meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let us see to it that the recollection of those whom we have lost becomes a pleasant memory to us'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Seneca: Letter 63, §4, on grief for lost friends. The English wording is translator Richard M. Gummere’s, from the 1917 Loeb edition.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & adviser to Nero
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and locatable to the sentence. It opens §4 of Letter 63, “On Grief for Lost Friends,” in Seneca’s Moral Letters to Lucilius — in Latin, Id agamus ut iucunda nobis amissorum fiat recordatio. The familiar English wording is Richard M. Gummere’s, from his 1917 Loeb Classical Library translation; Seneca wrote no English, so the sentence people share is the translator’s phrasing of Seneca’s thought.

source.heading: The source, located

docMeta.dd: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius)
Id agamus ut iucunda nobis amissorum fiat recordatio.
Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, vol. 1 — London: Heinemann; New York: Putnam’s, 1917

source.excerpt: Let us see to it that the recollection of those whom we have lost becomes a pleasant memory to us. No man reverts with pleasure to any subject which he will not be able to reflect upon without pain. So too it cannot but be that the names of those whom we have loved and lost come back to us with a sort of sting; but there is a pleasure even in this sting.
trail: The English sentence sits at §4 of Letter 63 in the Wikisource text of the Moral Letters ↗, which credits Richard Mott Gummere as translator and is transcribed from the scan of Ad Lucilium epistulae morales, volume 1.

The Latin behind it — Id agamus ut iucunda nobis amissorum fiat recordatio, followed by Nemo libenter ad id redit quod non sine tormento cogitaturus est — appears at LXIII.4 in the Latin text of Epistulae LXIII–LXIX ↗.

The edition record for that volume — Seneca, translated by Richard Mott Gummere, published by William Heinemann and G. P. Putnam’s Sons, London and New York, 1917, volume 1 of 3 — is given on Wikisource’s index page for the scan ↗, and the scan itself is on the Internet Archive ↗.
Wikiquote’s Seneca the Younger page ↗ carries Letter LXIII among its sourced quotations, and lists nothing about this line in its disputed or misattributed material.
source.excerptNote: Gummere’s 1917 English. The letter is addressed to Lucilius on the death of his friend Flaccus; §5 gives the same idea in the words of Seneca’s teacher Attalus.

source.rightsNote: Two layers, both clear. Seneca’s Latin, written around AD 62–65, has been in the public domain for centuries. The English wording quoted here is Richard M. Gummere’s translation, first published in 1917 ↗ — before 1931, so it too is public domain in the United States. Later translations of the same passage are a separate matter and may still be in copyright.

author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Stoic philosopher, tragedian and Roman statesman who became Nero’s tutor in AD 49 and his adviser from 54 to 62. Forced out of public life, he spent his last years writing the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilius — 124 surviving letters composed roughly between AD 62 and 65, addressed to Lucilius Junior, then procurator of Sicily, but plainly written for a wider readership. In AD 65 he was implicated in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero and ordered to take his own life.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Seneca. What travels badly is everything around it: the wording is a translator’s, and the sentence is almost never carried with the source that would let anyone check it.

items.why: Seneca wrote Id agamus ut iucunda nobis amissorum fiat recordatio (Latin text, Epistula LXIII.4 ↗). The 28 English words everyone shares are Gummere’s rendering, first published in the Loeb Classical Library in 1917 (edition record ↗). Other translators phrase it differently; none of the phrasings is Seneca’s.

Goodreads, for instance, lists the line under “Seneca, Complete Works of Seneca the Younger” with no letter number, translator or page ↗ — which is a pointer to roughly a thousand pages rather than a citation.

Lifted on its own it reads as gentle encouragement. In place it is the premise of a hard-edged Stoic argument: the very next sentence is “No man reverts with pleasure to any subject which he will not be able to reflect upon without pain” (Letter 63 ↗) — i.e. make the memory bearable or you will stop visiting it at all.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: genuinely Seneca the Younger, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 63, §4 ↗ — quoted in English in Richard M. Gummere’s 1917 Loeb translation.

context.heading: Why Seneca wrote it
lead: Letter 63 is a condolence note. Seneca opens it bluntly — “I am grieved to hear that your friend Flaccus is dead, but I would not have you sorrow more than is fitting” — and then argues his way toward this sentence. His claim is not that grief should be suppressed but that it should be metabolised: the memory of a dead friend is a thing you have to make survivable, because, as the very next line says, no one willingly returns to a thought that can only be thought in pain.

To make the point stick he hands the argument to his own teacher. Attalus, Seneca reports, used to say that remembering lost friends is pleasant the way some fruits are agreeably sour, or the way the bitterness of a very old wine is exactly what you enjoy in it — and that once enough time has passed, the part that stung burns off and only the pleasure reaches you. It is one of the least clinical passages in Stoic writing, and Seneca closes the letter by admitting he mourned a friend of his own badly.
detailsBody: The letter belongs to the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, the sequence of 124 surviving letters Seneca wrote in the last two or three years of his life, roughly AD 62–65. They are addressed to Lucilius Junior, procurator of Sicily, but they read as open letters — essays with a named recipient rather than private correspondence.

Grief was not an incidental topic for Seneca. Later in the same letter he names Annaeus Serenus as someone whose death he himself mourned deeply, which is why the advice arrives with an apology attached rather than as a lecture.
context.pull: The remembrance of lost friends is pleasant in the same way that certain fruits have an agreeably acid taste.
